title: Not everyone agreed
hook: Crescas and Albo proposed other lists; the streams read the principles differently

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last four foundations, and your line: I believe with complete faith. Did a hope start fresh for you? Today, the people who read the same list and answered back. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-seven.

Three. Not thirteen. A Spanish rabbi named Joseph Albo read Maimonides' list carefully, with respect, and then wrote a whole book arguing that Judaism rests on three roots. Tradition says Albo studied with another sharp reader, Hasdai Crescas, who questioned the list from a different angle. Neither one walked away from Judaism. They stayed inside it and argued about its foundations. Today's lesson is in the title, and it's a habit this tradition keeps.
screen: `THREE, NOT THIRTEEN.` → `READ WITH RESPECT, ANSWERED BACK.` → `ARGUING FROM INSIDE.`

segments.voice: Not everyone agreed. Start with Crescas. In his book, The Light of the LORD, he asked a hard question about the very first principle. The Torah gives commandments. But can you command someone to believe God exists? A command already assumes someone is commanding. So for Crescas, God's existence is the ground the commandments stand on, not one more item among them. He sorted beliefs differently, into roots, foundations and true beliefs, not one flat list. Next, Albo. His book is called Sefer HaIkkarim, the Book of Roots. He kept many of Maimonides' ideas but counted only three roots: God exists, the Torah is from heaven, and there is reward and punishment. The others, he said, grow out of these, like branches from a trunk. Then, the streams today. Some Jews hold the thirteen as written, and say them as written. Some read certain lines, such as the dead living again or the Torah from heaven, in other ways. Some put practice and community at the center and hold belief more loosely. Each says why, from its own reading of the tradition. And notice one more thing. The arguers didn't throw the list away. They kept it on the table, so they could keep arguing with it. Agreeing on which questions matter can hold a people together, even when the answers differ. Not everyone agreed.
screen: `CRESCAS: CAN BELIEF BE COMMANDED?` · `ALBO: THREE ROOTS, NOT THIRTEEN.` · `THE STREAMS READ THE LIST DIFFERENTLY.` · `THE LIST STAYS ON THE TABLE.` · then, large: `NOT EVERYONE AGREED.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to name your own foundations, if you'd like to. Settle, and let your breath slow. Ask yourself, quietly: what do I stand on? Not what I'm supposed to say. What actually holds me up on a hard day. It might be a belief, a person, a promise, a practice. See if you can find two or three. There's no right number. Maimonides counted thirteen and Albo counted three. Later, if you like, write them down. For now, rest on them, and stay with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Not everyone agreed. Crescas questioned the list, Albo counted three roots, and Jews today read the principles in different ways. Today's word.

Your line: not everyone agreed. Today, when you disagree with someone you respect, try what Albo did: say first what you take from them, then what you'd count differently. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-seven.

howItsDone: Jewish students read Maimonides' principles alongside the works of his critics, such as Crescas's Or Adonai and Albo's Sefer HaIkkarim; the different movements of Judaism explain in their own writings how they understand the principles.
